Short answer: All chemicals are like that. A reactions occurs much more readily when there is extra heat in the water. Hotter the liquid, the more readily things react.

Long answer: It actually has very little to do with hydrophilic/hydrophobic interactions directly. This is a fatty acid. See that O C, it really hates being in water. See that long chain of C O it really likes being in water. Hydrophilic/hydrophobic interactions are when a charges on a molecule dictate where and how the molecule forms. Think of it as throwing a children's pool party. Some children really like being in the pool, and some children really hate it. Over time the children that like being in the pool will go in and remain there and the children that do not will go in and then come out. This has nothing to do with why chocolate is mixing, but is a fun aside.

The reason that chocolate is mixing more readily is the amount of free energy inside of the liquid. The act of the mix breaking apart takes energy, it takes energy to keep the mix separated, and it takes energy to dissolve the mix into the liquid. Heat is a form of free energy as well as stirring is a kinetic form of free energy. Think of the water as little workers and the free energy as money. More money means more workers have access to the mix, and more money means that each worker is paid more and thus is working harder. It does not really matter, to you lay person, if this money is cash (heat) or check (kinetic). Each chemical reaction requires a unique amount of energy known as the activation energy. When the liquid is hotter it is starting with a higher base amount of energy thus needs less additional energy put into the liquid from stirring. This is why hotter liquids cause things to dissolve more readily then colder liquids, and why the majority of home chemical reactions (tea, coffee, hot chocolate) are done at high temperatures.
